## Tutorial 0: Warm-up - random graphs, a bridge from Week 5
  
### 0.1 Simulating an Erdős-Rényi graph
  
  Before we touch any real data, let's do what Week 5 trained us to do
first: write down a generating process and simulate from it.

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
n <- 50
p <- 0.06

g_er <- play_erdos_renyi(n, p, directed = FALSE)

set.seed(1)
ggraph(g_er, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_node_point(size = 2) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = paste0("Erdos-Renyi random graph: n = ", n, ", p = ", p))
```

**Exercise 0.1** - Regenerate `g_er` with (a) the same `n` but a
smaller `p`, and (b) the same `p` but a larger `n`. In one sentence
each, describe how the plot changes. Which parameter controls how
*dense* the network looks, and which controls how *big* it looks?

### 0.2 Degree distribution vs the Poisson overlay

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
n <- 300; p <- 0.02
g_er2 <- play_erdos_renyi(n, p, directed = FALSE) |>
  activate(nodes) |> mutate(degree = centrality_degree())

deg_df <- g_er2 |> activate(nodes) |> as_tibble()
lambda <- (n - 1) * p

ggplot(deg_df, aes(degree)) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = after_stat(prop)), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(degree = 0:15, prop = dpois(0:15, lambda)),
             aes(degree, prop), colour = "firebrick", size = 2) +
  labs(title = paste0("Empirical degree distribution vs Poisson(",
                       round(lambda, 1), ")"),
       x = "Degree", y = "Proportion of nodes") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Exercise 0.2** - This should look familiar: it's Week 5's "many
identical outbreaks" logic, applied to a *pair of nodes* instead of a
*case count*. In 2/3 sentences, explain in your own words why each
node's degree in $G(n,p)$ is approximately Poisson-distributed for
large $n$ and small $p$. (Hint: think about the $n-1$ independent
                          coin-flips each node makes.)

**Exercise 0.3** - Increase `p` to 0.1 while keeping `n = 300`, so
$np$ is no longer small. Does the Poisson overlay still fit well? Why
or why not (what assumption behind the Poisson approximation starts
            to break)?
  
### 0.3 A heavier-tailed alternative
  
```{r}
set.seed(2026)
g_ba <- igraph::sample_pa(n = 150, power = 1, m = 1, directed = FALSE) |>
  as_tbl_graph() |>
  activate(nodes) |> mutate(degree = centrality_degree())

ba_df <- g_ba |> activate(nodes) |> as_tibble()

ggplot(ba_df, aes(degree)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "darkorange", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Barabasi-Albert (preferential attachment) degree distribution",
       subtitle = "Note the log y-axis: a few very high-degree hubs",
       x = "Degree", y = "Count (log scale)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Exercise 0.4** - Compare this histogram to the Erdős-Rényi one from
0.2 (same `x` axis, roughly the same `n`). In 2/3 sentences: which
model would you pick as a *contact network* for an infectious disease,
and what does the answer imply about how a single highly-connected
individual could affect an outbreak? Keep this answer. You will want it
again in Week 8.

## Tutorial 1: Building and plotting a basic network

### 1.1 A small dataset

We'll use a small, easy-to-inspect network to start. Either use the
built-in `highschool` dataset (igraph/ggraph) or a dataset you've
prepared (e.g. co-authorship, contact network from a previous course).

```{r}
data(highschool, package = "ggraph")
head(highschool)
```

```{r}
g <- as_tbl_graph(highschool, directed = FALSE)
g
```

**Exercise 1.1** - Inspect `g |> activate(nodes) |> as_tibble()` and
`g |> activate(edges) |> as_tibble()`. How many nodes and edges are
there? Is the network directed or undirected? Does that match your
expectation given the data?

### 1.2 Moving between representations

```{r}
adj <- igraph::as_adjacency_matrix(g, sparse = FALSE)
adj[1:6, 1:6]
```

**Exercise 1.2** - Confirm for yourself that the edge list and the
adjacency matrix carry the same information: pick any two pupils who
appear connected in `adj`, and check that the corresponding row exists
in `g |> activate(edges) |> as_tibble()`. Which representation would
you reach for if you needed to quickly look up *all of one pupil's
friends*. Why?
  
  ### 1.3 A default plot
  
```{r}
set.seed(1)
ggraph(g, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_node_point(size = 2) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Highschool friendship network (force-directed)")
```

### 1.4 Trying different layouts

**Exercise 1.3** - Produce the same plot with at least three different
`layout` arguments to `ggraph()` (try `"fr"`, `"circle"`, `"kk"`,
                                  `"stress"`; see `?layout_tbl_graph` for options). Arrange them with
`patchwork` for comparison. For each, write one sentence: what
structure (if any) becomes more or less visible?
  
  > **Reproducibility checkpoint**: record the seed used for any
> stochastic layout (e.g. `"fr"`) so the figure can be regenerated
> identically.

### 1.5 Summary statistics beyond degree

```{r}
tibble::tibble(
  density    = igraph::edge_density(g),
  n_nodes    = igraph::vcount(g),
  n_edges    = igraph::ecount(g),
  components = igraph::components(g)$no
)
```

> **Note**: we call `igraph::` functions directly on `g` here rather
> than routing through `dplyr::summarise()`. The latter needs a
> `summarise.tbl_graph` method to be found via S3 dispatch, which can
> silently fail with `no applicable method for 'summarise'` if your R
> session doesn't have `tidygraph` fully attached when you run the
> chunk in isolation. Calling `igraph::` functions sidesteps that
> entirely. A `tbl_graph` *is* an `igraph` object underneath.

**Exercise 1.4** - Compute the same four statistics for your
Erdős-Rényi graph `g_er` from Tutorial 0 (same `n` as `highschool` if
you want a fair comparison; regenerate with `n = igraph::vcount(g)`).
Which statistic differs most between the real and simulated network,
and what does that tell you about how "friendship" networks differ
from purely random ones?

## Tutorial 2: Encoding attributes

### 2.1 Computing node attributes

```{r}
g2 <- g |>
  activate(nodes) |>
  mutate(
    degree = centrality_degree(),
    component = as.factor(group_components())
  )

g2 |> activate(nodes) |> as_tibble() |> head()
```

### 2.2 Encoding degree as size and colour

```{r}
set.seed(1)
ggraph(g2, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_node_point(aes(size = degree, colour = degree)) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 6) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Node degree encoded as size and colour")
```

**Exercise 2.1** - The plot above uses *both* size and colour for the
same variable (degree), a redundant encoding. Produce two alternative
versions: (a) size only, (b) colour only (constant size). In 2/3
sentences, discuss whether the redundant encoding in the original is
helpful or unnecessary here, and whether your answer would change for
a colourblind reader (consider `scale_colour_viridis_c()` vs a
red-green palette).

### 2.3 A second centrality measure

Degree isn't the only way to describe "importance" in a network.

```{r}
g2 <- g2 |>
  mutate(betweenness = centrality_betweenness())

g2 |> activate(nodes) |> as_tibble() |>
  ggplot(aes(degree, betweenness)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Degree vs betweenness centrality",
       x = "Degree", y = "Betweenness") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Exercise 2.2** - Find the pupil(s) with high betweenness but only
moderate degree. In 1-2 sentences, explain in plain language what that
combination means about their position in the friendship network
(hint: think "bridge between groups" rather than "popular"). This
distinction matters directly for epidemic modelling: which kind of
node would you rather vaccinate first, and why? (No need to compute 
anything further, just reason about it from the definitions.)

### 2.4 Edge attributes: worked examples

Two worked examples, one for a continuous weight and one for a
categorical attribute. Both reuse `g` from Tutorial 1.

**Weight → width**
  
```{r}
edge_weights <- highschool |>
  count(from, to, name = "weight")

g_w <- as_tbl_graph(edge_weights, directed = FALSE)

set.seed(1)
ggraph(g_w, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = weight), alpha = 0.4, colour = "steelblue") +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.3, 2.5)) +
  geom_node_point(size = 1.5) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Edge width = number of years a friendship was reported",
       edge_width = "Weight")
```

`count(from, to)` collapses the 1957/1958 edge list into one weighted
edge per pair; `scale_edge_width(range = ...)` caps how extreme the
width contrast gets. An uncapped scale makes a 2x weight difference
look far more dramatic than it is.

**Category → colour**
  
```{r}
g_year <- as_tbl_graph(highschool, directed = FALSE)

set.seed(1)
ggraph(g_year, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(colour = factor(year)), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_node_point(size = 1.5, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_edge_colour_manual(values = c("steelblue", "firebrick")) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Edge colour = survey year", edge_colour = "Year")
```

Here the edge attribute is **categorical**, not a magnitude, so
colour (not width) is the natural channel: width would falsely
imply 1957 and 1958 sit on an ordered "more/less" scale.

**Exercise 2.3** - Using the two examples above as a template:
  
  (a) Produce a version of the width plot with `scale_edge_width()`'s
`range` argument *removed* (i.e. let ggraph pick the default range).
Compare it to the capped version above: does the uncapped version
overstate the weight-2 edges?

(b) Produce a version of the colour plot that instead maps `year` to
**alpha** rather than colour (e.g. `geom_edge_link(aes(alpha =
factor(year)))`). In 1/2 sentences, is alpha a good substitute for
colour here, or does it lose information the colour version kept?

(c) If your own dataset has a natural edge weight or category instead
of `year`, repeat whichever of the two examples fits, and note one
design decision you had to make that didn't come up with the
`highschool` data.

### 2.5 Applying course styling

**Exercise 2.4** - Apply the colour palette, font, and theme
conventions you've used in earlier weeks to one of your network plots
above. Note any places where the conventions "don't quite work" for
network plots (e.g. does `theme_void()` conflict with a custom theme
that sets axis text?) and how you resolved it.

## Tutorial 3 (double session): Alternatives to node-link diagrams, and uncertainty about network statistics

### Short session: Adjacency matrix view

```{r}
library(reshape2)

adj <- as.matrix(igraph::as_adjacency_matrix(g))
adj_df <- melt(adj)

ggplot(adj_df, aes(Var1, Var2, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank()) +
  labs(title = "Adjacency matrix: highschool network",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Edge")
```

**Exercise 3.1** - The order of nodes in the matrix above is arbitrary
(the order they appear in the data). Reorder nodes by `component` or by
`degree` (e.g. using `arrange()` on the node table before extracting
the adjacency matrix, or reindexing rows/columns of `adj`). Does
reordering reveal block structure that wasn't visible before?

### Long session (after break)

#### Arc diagram

```{r}
# A simple arc diagram using ggraph's "linear" layout
set.seed(1)
ggraph(g2, layout = "linear") +
  geom_edge_arc(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = component), size = 2) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Arc diagram, nodes in default order")
```

**Exercise 3.2** - Reorder nodes (e.g. `mutate(g2, ... ) |> arrange(component)`
before plotting, or use the `sort.by` argument if available in your
layout) so that nodes in the same component are adjacent. Compare the
"default order" and "sorted by component" arc diagrams. Which is more
informative, and why?

#### Comparative critique

**Exercise 3.3** - Using the *same* network (highschool or your own),
produce three plots side by side: (1) node-link (best layout from
Tutorial 1), (2) adjacency matrix (best ordering from above), (3) arc
diagram (best ordering from above). Write a structured comparison
(~200 words) addressing:

- Which representation best shows **overall density** of the network?
- Which best shows **community/cluster structure**?
- Which would you choose for an audience **unfamiliar** with network
  diagrams, and why?
- Reference Kolaczyk & Csárdi and/or the Handbook of Data Visualization
  in your answer.

### Bridge from Week 6: a network statistic is a point estimate too

A single computed network statistic (mean degree, one node's
centrality) came from **one observed network**. Just as with a sample
mean in Week 6, we can ask: how much would this number change if we'd
observed a slightly different network?

#### 3.4 Bootstrapping the mean degree

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
boot_mean_degree <- function(g) {
  nodes_tbl <- g |> activate(nodes) |> as_tibble()
  n <- nrow(nodes_tbl)
  resampled <- sample(seq_len(n), n, replace = TRUE)
  sub <- igraph::induced_subgraph(g, unique(resampled))
  mean(igraph::degree(sub))
}

boot_dist <- replicate(500, boot_mean_degree(g))
head(boot_dist)
```

**Exercise 3.4** - Plot `boot_dist` as (a) a histogram and (b) a
density curve, reusing your Week 6 Tutorial code directly (this is
literally the same bootstrap-then-visualise pipeline, applied to a
new statistic). Report the 90% bootstrap interval
(`quantile(boot_dist, c(0.05, 0.95))`) and state in one sentence what
this interval represents ("if we resampled nodes this way many times,
90% of the resulting mean-degree estimates would fall in this range").

#### 3.5 Don't dynamite-plot it

```{r}
summ <- data.frame(mean = mean(boot_dist), se = sd(boot_dist))

p_dynamite <- ggplot(summ, aes(x = "Highschool net", y = mean)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey70", width = 0.4) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.1) +
  labs(title = "Bad: bar + error bar", x = NULL, y = "Mean degree") +
  theme_minimal()

p_dots <- ggplot(data.frame(x = boot_dist), aes(x)) +
  ggdist::stat_dotsinterval(quantiles = 50, fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Better: quantile dotplot", x = "Mean degree") +
  theme_minimal()

p_dynamite + p_dots
```

**Exercise 3.5** - In 3/4 sentences: what does the dynamite-plot
version of this figure hide that the dotplot version shows? Then
identify which *kind* of uncertainty this bootstrap actually
represents. Is it closer to Week 6's **sampling uncertainty** (as if
the highschool pupils were a sample from a larger population) or to
Week 5's **simulation variability** (as if the network itself were one
draw from a random-graph model)? Justify your answer, and note that
the two framings would call for different-looking captions even though
the plot code is identical.

#### 3.6 Comparing degree distributions across node types (violin)

```{r}
g2 |> activate(nodes) |> as_tibble() |>
  ggplot(aes(component, degree)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Degree distribution by connected component",
       x = "Component", y = "Degree") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Exercise 3.6** - Is there a component whose degree distribution
looks meaningfully different in shape (not just mean) from the others)?
Would a bar-plus-error-bar summary have shown you this? Use this as a
second, worked example of the Week 6 "show more of the distribution"
principle applied to network data.

## Tutorial 4 (optional extension): A first taste of spread on a network

This section previews Week 8. It's optional this week, but the code
you write here will drop almost unchanged into next week's capstone.

### 4.1 A branching process, constrained by structure

Week 5's branching process assumed anyone could infect anyone. Here,
infection can only travel along edges of a contact network.

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
n <- 60
g_contact <- play_erdos_renyi(n, p = 0.06, directed = FALSE)
adj <- as.matrix(igraph::as_adjacency_matrix(g_contact))

simulate_on_network <- function(adj, p_infect = 0.3, max_steps = 15) {
  n <- nrow(adj)
  infected <- rep(FALSE, n); infected[sample(n, 1)] <- TRUE
  new_cases <- sum(infected)
  for (t in 1:max_steps) {
    current <- which(infected)
    candidates <- which(!infected)
    would_infect <- sapply(candidates, function(j) {
      neighbours_infected <- sum(adj[j, current] == 1)
      runif(1) < 1 - (1 - p_infect)^neighbours_infected
    })
    newly <- candidates[would_infect]
    if (length(newly) == 0) break
    infected[newly] <- TRUE
    new_cases <- c(new_cases, length(newly))
  }
  new_cases
}

curve <- simulate_on_network(adj)

ggplot(data.frame(step = seq_along(curve), new_cases = curve),
       aes(step, new_cases)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(title = "New cases per step, spread constrained to network edges",
       x = "Step", y = "New cases") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Exercise 4.1** - Run `simulate_on_network()` with several different
seeds, keeping `adj`, `p_infect`, and `max_steps` fixed. Plot the
resulting curves as a small-multiples panel (`facet_wrap`), the same
way Week 5 Tutorial 2 handled many random-walk realisations. Do some
runs fizzle out almost immediately while others take off, even though
every run used the *same* network and the *same* infection
probability?

**Exercise 4.2 (extension)** - Repeat Exercise 4.1 but swap `g_contact`
for the Barabási-Albert graph `g_ba` from Tutorial 0 (rebuild `adj`
accordingly). Does an outbreak starting at a random node behave
differently on a heavy-tailed contact network than on an
Erdős-Rényi one? What if you deliberately start the outbreak at the
highest-degree node instead of a random one (`which.max(degree(...))`
)? Keep your code and your answer. Week 8's capstone builds a full
S/I/R model and a multi-run ribbon plot directly on top of this
pattern.

### Looking ahead to Week 8

Next week we add two new dimensions to networks: **space** (nodes have
geographic coordinates, edges drawn on maps) and **time** (networks
that evolve, e.g. epidemic spread). The representation/encoding
choices from this week (node-link vs matrix vs arc, attribute
encodings) still apply. But they are now layered onto a basemap or a sequence
of snapshots. Your Tutorial 3 bootstrap code and your Tutorial 4
network-constrained branching process are both direct inputs to Week
8's capstone figure, which combines simulation (Week 5), uncertainty
(Week 6), and network visualisation (Week 7) into a single multi-panel
figure with space and time layered on top.
